Three Cats, One Rabies Outbreak: What Happens Next?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1447 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Catster

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you.
  • Every time the topic of vaccines comes up, thereâs always someone who questions whether our pets really need them.
  • Industry observers note that rabies is a perfect example.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Every time the topic of vaccines comes up, thereâs always someone who questions whether our pets really need them. Asking questions about medical care is perfectly reasonable (in fact, informed pet parents should!), but dismissing vaccination without understanding the risks is another story.

Industry observers note that rabies is a perfect example. This is not some historical disease or something that only affects animals in remote areas or underdeveloped countries. It can infect mammals, including our own cats, dogs, and even us. Whatâs even scarier is that once the clinical signs appear, rabies is almost always fatal, making prevention essential.

Sources indicate that recent events in Quebec offer a timely reminder. Amid an emerging wildlife outbreak, three domestic cats tested positive for raccoon-strain rabies in 2026. Although these numbers pale in comparison to the number of infected wildlife recorded since December 20241, it demonstrates how a disease circulating in wild animals can reach our pets.

Recent findings suggest that and this isn't just a Canadian concern. Rabies variants and wildlife risks differ by region, but keeping pets appropriately vaccinated is a responsibility shared by pet parents everywhere.

Despite its name, raccoon-strain rabies isn't exclusive to raccoons; they are simply the reservoir species of this particular variant of the rabies virus. Skunks and other mammals â including cats â can also become infected.

It has been revealed that rabies attacks the central nervous system. It spreads mainly through the bite of an infected animal, when virus-containing saliva enters the body. Saliva can also transmit the virus if it reaches an open wound, the eyes, nose, or mouth.

Raccoon rabies had been eliminated in Quebec following an outbreak between 2006 and 2009, but the virus resurfaced in 2024. Since then, more outbreaks have appeared, and case numbers have climbed sharply in 2026, particularly in MontÃ©rÃ©gie. By October 29, 328 animals had tested positive for raccoon-strain rabies across the province. The three infected cats are examples of how a virus circulating in wildlife can also reach our pets, even though cats are not the main reservoir responsible for spreading this variant.

Cats are naturally curious, territorial predators. They investigate unfamiliar scents, watch moving animals, explore hidden spaces, and sometimes pursue creatures that would be better left alone. These behaviors are normal expressions of feline biology, not evidence that a cat is being reckless.

Unfortunately, wildlife encounters can turn dangerous very quickly. A raccoon searching for food near a house may cross paths with an outdoor cat. A skunk hiding beneath a shed may be investigated by a curious feline. Even a sick or disoriented wild animal can catch a cat's attention, and one of the hallmarks of rabies infection in wild animals is a reduced fear of humans and predators as the infection attacks the nervous system. And cats being cats, curiosity can get them into trouble! These encounters don't just happen deep in the woods. A backyard, garage, or garden fence can be enough.

One of the infected cats was believed to have contracted rabies after contact with a wild animal. Another case led to three people receiving preventive treatment following possible exposure.

It has been revealed that rabies doesn't always turn an animal into a movie villain, either. Early signs can be subtle, which is why recognizing unusual behavior and reporting possible exposure is so key.

When people think of rabies, they often picture a snarling animal, dripping saliva, and attacking everything in sight. Hollywood certainly loves that version! Unfortunately, rabies doesn't always come with such obvious special effects.

Recent findings suggest that in cats, the first signs can be surprisingly subtle. A normally friendly kitty may suddenly become grumpy, hide more than usual, vocalize differently, lose interest in food, or behave in ways that seem completely out of character. Since cats are already experts at keeping their humans guessing, a sudden behavior change can sometimes be easy to dismiss. But when a cat starts acting noticeably different from their usual, wonderfully weird self, it's worth paying attention.

According to recent reports, as the disease progresses, neurological signs become more apparent. Affected cats may become disoriented, walk unsteadily, have difficulty swallowing, drool excessively, develop weakness, or eventually become paralyzed. Some become unusually aggressive or sensitive to touch, sounds, and light.

In a recent development, there is also a less dramatic presentation called paralytic rabies, sometimes referred to as âdumb rabiesâ. Instead of becoming aggressive, affected animals may become unusually quiet, weak, or withdrawn. Difficulty swallowing, a drooping jaw, and progressive paralysis can follow. So no, a rabid animal doesn't necessarily look like it's auditioning for a horror movie.

Recent findings suggest that of course, these signs can also occur with other neurological conditions, injuries, and intoxications. Nobody should attempt to diagnose rabies based on behavior alone. A cat showing sudden, unexplained neurological changes needs prompt veterinary attention, particularly if wildlife exposure is possible.

Recent findings suggest that here's another catch: rabies can take weeks, sometimes even months, to show itself. A cat may seem perfectly fine after an encounter with an infected animal, but that doesn't mean the virus isn't already in its body. So if a possible exposure happens, don't wait for your cat to look sick before calling the vet. By then, it may be too late.

Sadly, once rabies reaches the clinical stage, there is no cure, and the outcome is almost always fatal. That's why a suspected exposure should never be a wait-and-see situation. Don't wait for signs to appear; contact your veterinarian right away. With rabies, prevention isn't just better than treatment; it's our best chance to protect our cats in the first place.

Industry observers note that think your indoor cat doesn't need a rabies vaccine? Think again! Indoor cats have fewer opportunities to encounter wildlife, but escapes happen, doors get left open, and sometimes wildlife finds its way indoors. Nobody plans these little adventures, least of all the cat!

In a recent development, rabies vaccination is also required by law for cats in many countries and jurisdictions. Even where it isn't mandatory, keeping your cat vaccinated is an notable part of preventive care. Ask your veterinarian about the appropriate schedule for your cat.

Recent findings suggest that and remember, vaccination doesn't mean ignoring a possible exposure. If your vaccinated cat is bitten by a potentially rabid animal, contact your veterinarian right away.

Industry observers note that if your cat is bitten or scratched by a wild animal, contact your veterinarian immediately, even if your cat seems perfectly fine. Bite wounds can hide beneath all that lovely fur, and waiting for signs to appear is not an option.

Keep your cat away from other animals and don't try to catch or handle the wild animal. Report suspicious wildlife to local authorities and let trained professionals deal with it.

Recent findings suggest that if a person is bitten or scratched, or infected saliva enters an open wound or contacts the eyes, nose, or mouth, wash the area thoroughly with soap and running water for 15 minutes and seek medical attention immediately. Post-exposure treatment can prevent rabies from developing, so don't delay.

And please, leave dead wildlife alone. No bare-handed investigations or impromptu rescue missions!

Quebec is also fighting the outbreak through wildlife surveillance and vaccination campaigns using vaccine baits. These efforts help protect wild animals and reduce further spread.

Cats will be cats. A rustling bush can become the most fascinating thing in the universe, and a passing raccoon may look like an invitation to investigate. We can't blame them for being curious. We can give them safer ways to enjoy their adventures.

#9254. Why Birds Peck Windows in Fall – the Real Reasons Revealed by Experts

Why Birds Peck Windows in Fall – the Real Reasons Revealed by Experts

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1468 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Folk have long discussed why backyard birds peck windows in fall, and once Google got involved, plenty more possible causes were added to the pile.
  • Sources indicate that some of the most common speculations about why birds tap windows include attempting to get your attention when it's time to refill feeders, impending bad news, small songbirds wanting to come into the warm, and a message from a passed loved one.
  • Whether you find the tap-tap-tapping of your beneficial garden friends endearing or highly annoying, once you understand the real reasons avian experts say are behind window pecking, you can better support your garden birds in fall.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Folk have long discussed why backyard birds peck windows in fall, and once Google got involved, plenty more possible causes were added to the pile. Now research and observations from bird experts have revealed the real reasons behind this bizarre behaviour, and you may be surprised to learn what they are.

Sources indicate that some of the most common speculations about why birds tap windows include attempting to get your attention when it's time to refill feeders, impending bad news, small songbirds wanting to come into the warm, and a message from a passed loved one. Avian experts, however, have put forward reasons based on cold, hard data, and they provide a fascinating insight into fall bird behaviour.

Whether you find the tap-tap-tapping of your beneficial garden friends endearing or highly annoying, once you understand the real reasons avian experts say are behind window pecking, you can better support your garden birds in fall. Understanding the likely causes will also help you decide if should take action to stop the window tapping to save birds from harm, and save your sanity, too.

As temperatures decrease in fall, insects become more scarce, many birds are forced to forage for food in new areas. Because glass retains heat from the sun as well as windows allowing some of a home’s heat to escape, any tiny gaps in frames become welcoming nooks for insects to enter diapause (similar to hibernation) – and consequently, one of those spots hungry birds may favor. You might think modern windows don’t offer much space for critters to hole up in, but those drainage weep holes and sliding tracks provide plenty of opportunities. Spiders also use window corners to spin insect-catching webs and lay eggs, offering further protein-rich food to the bird buffet.

According to the British Trust for Ornithology (BTO), there’s a rise in birds pecking at windows for food in fall and winter, and in particular by the tit family which includes chickadees and titmice. The organisation also cites that birds may pick at traditional window putty as it’s made with fish or linseed oil, both a valuable source of energy in colder months.

Industry observers note that research carried out by the Cornell Lab of Ornithology found that the lower angle of sunlight hitting windows in fall significantly increases how reflective the glass is. Aside from birds having no concept of what a window is, our feathered friends see differently to us. Most birds have eyes on the sides of their heads to give them almost-360° vision, and while that’s highly useful for spotting potential predators, it means their forward vision isn’t as good as ours. So, reflections in windows are easily interpreted as extra habitat and when birds encounter the glass – which in fall, especially, can appear to them as an invisible barrier – they may peck at it repeatedly to investigate.

Fall is when juvenile birds disperse, and these inexperienced youngsters have a lot to learn about the world around them, and much spatial awareness still to develop. Data published by the American Bird Conservancy and the US Fish & Wildlife Service shows a strong rise in what they term ‘glass interactions’ in fall. While many of these will be window collisions caused by mirror-like glass and navigational error, some will be window pecking led by curiosity as birds investigate their surroundings.

Recent findings suggest that while territorial behaviour among most of our feathered friends peaks in spring, many resident birds claim their territory in fall, according to the National Audubon Society. Northern cardinals, non-migrating American robins, northern mockingbirds, towhees and bluebirds are all highly territorial through fall into winter. And there's a very good reason for this, because as summer broods disperse, thousands of juvenile birds search a new territory. In the face of this competition, existing populations fiercely defend their established territories – especially if it contains a valuable food source such as a garden shrub hung with berries birds love through winter!

According to recent reports, with windows becoming mirror-like in the low fall sun, dominant birds can attack their own reflection, mistaking it for a competitor. So this is a common reason why birds tap windows in fall as well as spring.

Whether you have a towhee aggressively pecking at your patio doors or a chickadee tap-tapping your bedroom window at all hours, now you understand what’s behind this behaviour, you can do something about it. Gentle pecking for food harms neither bird nor human, so it’s safe to ignore this low-level behaviour. But more insistent pecking at a window, fighting imagined aggressors or attempting to break through an invisible barrier is not just highly annoying to us but harmful to birds, damaging beaks and wasting valuable energy.

It has been revealed that taking action to stop birds pecking windows involves making glass more visible, or keeping birds away from it in the first place. That means these solutions will also reduce the risk of feathered friends flying into windows and injuring themselves. By working out the likely reason behind a bird tapping on your window, you can choose the method that will be most effective.

In a recent development, your first step to stop birds tapping windows is to move any houseplants away from windows that are being targeted. To a young bird, a windowsill full of greenery can look like inviting habitat or contribute to the illusion that this could be a continuation of their flightpath.

A quick and cheap solution if the targeted window opens is to shut a length of double-sided reflective bird scare tape like this from Amazon in it. When the tape blows in the wind, its holographic surface casts erratic patterns of ultraviolet light which most birds perceive as a threat. For resident birds in search of tasty insects, this may be enough for them to deem that window an unsafe zone.

While the go-to for making windows more visible to birds and preventing collisions is decals, they're only effective if the gaps between them are narrow enough. A few decals dotted about on a large window are next to useless as birds will likely perceive the areas between them as possible flightpaths, just as they do the gaps between branches in woodland.

According to recent reports, A far simpler, more effective and still-stylish alternative is to create a grid of dots around 2 inches apart across the entire window. Use a white oil-based permanent marker like a Sharpie Medium Point Paint Marker, available from Amazon, and for a professional result, use a stencil template. You could make your own by punching holes in cardboard or save yourself the trouble with an Avi-Dot Bird Saver Window Stencil from Etsy.

Another effective way to help birds see house windows as a barrier is to stick on clear collision tape like CollidEscape, available from Amazon. To be effective against bird strikes, and therefore cut down on curious birds pecking at what they perceive as an invisible wall, you’ll need to position the tape in vertical or horizontal stripes with the edges no more than 2 inches apart. If you have feathered friends that often peck at a particular part of a window, this is a useful method as you can reduce the gap between strips here.

If a particular bird still persists in pecking at a window, creating a temporary cardboard barrier can help break the habit.

Sources indicate that if you have a problem with a particularly territorial or bigger bird such as a woodpecker or seagull, a final resort is to fix a permanent deterrent near to the targeted window. Wind-powered metal spinners throw out unpredictable flashes of light, visually confusing birds to create an area they perceive as unsafe. Windmill spinners like these Stainless Steel Bird Deterrent Devices by Ebern Designs on Wayfair mean you don’t have to compromise on garden style.

Backyard birds need our support more than ever once fall turns to winter, whether that's preventing a bird bath freezing over to preserve their water supply, saving up kitchen scraps to feed feathered friends, or making sure smaller songbirds get a fair share of food. Now you understand why birds tap on windows in fall, you can decide whether or not to ignore the behaviour or take action for your and the bird's benefit.

Emma is an avid gardener and has worked in media for over 25 years. Previously editor of Modern Gardens magazine, she regularly writes for the Royal Horticultural Society. She loves to garden hand-in-hand with nature and her garden is full of bees, butterflies and birds as well as cottage-garden blooms. As a keen natural crafter, her cutting patch and veg bed are increasingly being taken over by plants that can be dried or woven into a crafty project.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Artem Stryzhak, 36, a Ukrainian national, was sentenced today to 70 months in prison for conspiracy to commit computer fraud in connection with a series of ransomware attacks that targeted hospitals, government entities, law firms, and other businesses around the world.

“This sentence concludes a years-long, multi-continent investigation into a defendant who participated in cyber-attacks against Americans’ businesses and health care,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “Cybercriminals who terrorize American businesses cannot evade justice by operating from abroad or hiding behind sophisticated technology. Artem Stryzhak’s sentence underscores the Justice Department’s resolve to dismantle ransomware groups, hold them accountable, and protect American businesses and people from cyber extortion.”.

It has been revealed that “Ransomware attacks like those committed by the defendant wreak enormous havoc — harming victim companies that pay millions in remediation and ransoms, preventing hospitals and other critical facilities from accessing data, and putting sensitive information in the hands of bad actors,” stated U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. for the Eastern District of Latest York. “Today’s sentence reflects that cybercriminals cannot hide from law enforcement and will face significant punishment for their criminal conduct. We remain determined to capture Volodymyr Tymoshchuk, a serial ransomware developer and Stryzhak’s co-conspirator.”.

“Disrupting a ransomware group that attacked approximately 1,500 victims worldwide and sentencing a defendant who had targeted healthcare during the COVID-19 pandemic is of significant importance to this office,” stated U.S. Attorney Gregory W. Kehoe for the Middle District of Florida. “We are proud of our law enforcement partners for their skilled investigative work in bringing this criminal to justice.”.

According to recent reports, “Artem Stryzhak is a prolific cybercriminal who worked with multiple ransomware groups to target U.S. businesses and hospitals,” mentioned Operations Director Brett Leatherman of the FBI’s Cyber Branch. “These groups disrupted patient care and caused more than $100 million in losses. Today’s sentence reflects the seriousness of Stryzhak’s crimes and demonstrates the FBI’s global reach and extensive network of international partners. Multiple field offices contributed to this investigation, and our work does not end here. We will continue to leverage every tool at our disposal to track down Stryzhak’s co-conspirators and hold them accountable, including Volodymyr Viktorovych Tymoshchuk.”.

According to court documents, Stryzhak, formerly of Barcelona, Spain, conspired with others to perpetrate ransomware attacks on behalf of multiple ransomware groups against victim computer networks in the United States and other countries. The conspiracies caused significant damage to victim computer systems. Beginning in approximately June 2021, Stryzhak joined the ongoing Nefilim conspiracy as a Nefilim ransomware affiliate. Stryzhak was given access to the Nefilim ransomware and agreed with one of the Nefilim ransomware group administrators, Volodymyr Tymoshchuk, to pay the Nefilim administrators, including Tymoshchuk, 20% of the ransom proceeds extorted from victims in exchange for Stryzhak’s access to the Nefilim ransomware.

The ransomware attacks that Stryzhak conducted with Nefilim ransomware included a June 2021 attack in which Stryzhak stole data from a firm in the oil and gas transportation industry. About a week later, Stryzhak created email addresses that were incorporated in a ransom note sent to the victim company. Stryzhak conspired with the Nefilim ransomware actors until at least October 2021. If a victim paid the ransom demand, the perpetrators provided the decryption key, enabling the victim to decrypt files locked by the ransomware.

In a recent development, also according to court documents, Stryzhak separately joined the Hive ransomware group as one of its earliest affiliates. From June 2021 to January 2023, Hive conspirators attacked approximately 1,500 victims worldwide, including government entities, hospitals, and businesses. Hive ransomware attacks caused major disruptions in victim daily operations around the world and affected responses to the COVID-19 pandemic. In one case, a hospital attacked by the Hive ransomware group had to forgo digital technology to treat existing patients and was unable to accept upcoming patients immediately following the attack.

In his role as a Hive affiliate, Stryzhak and his co-conspirators deployed Hive ransomware against seven victims, including law firms, a dentist office, and a healthcare provider during the COVID-19 pandemic. Victims were unable to access their encrypted data. The FBI, as part of a months-long disruption campaign against the Hive ransomware group, provided a decryption key to one of Stryzhak’s victims, thereby allowing that victim to decrypt its encrypted data without having to pay a ransom.

Stryzhak was arrested in Spain in June 2024 and extradited to the United States in April 2025. Stryzhak pleaded guilty in December 2025 to two counts of conspiracy to commit fraud, extortion, and related activity in connection with computers.

It has been revealed that the FBI Springfield Field Office investigated the Nefilim ransomware case and the FBI Tampa Field Office investigated the Hive ransomware case. The Criminal Division’s Office of International Affairs, the FBI’s New York Field Office, and Spanish law enforcement authorities provided substantial assistance locating, arresting, and extraditing Stryzhak.

Recent findings suggest that acting Assistant Deputy Chief James S. Yoon of the Criminal Division’s Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section (CCIPS), former CCIPS Senior Trial Attorney Brian Z. Mund, and Assistant United States Attorneys Alexander F. Mindlin and Ellen H. Sise of the Eastern District of Latest York’s National Security and Cybercrime Section prosecuted the Nefilim ransomware case. CCIPS Trial Attorneys Alison M. Zitron and Christen M. Gallagher and Assistant United States Attorney Hannah Watson of the Middle District of Florida prosecuted the Hive ransomware case.

Industry observers note that the U.S. Department of State’s Transnational Organized Crime (TOC) Rewards Program has offered a reward of up to $11 million for information leading to the arrest and/or conviction or location of Stryzhak’s charged co-conspirator, Volodymyr Tymoshchuk. Anyone with information about Tymoshchuk should contact the FBI via phone at +1-917-242-1407, by email at TymoTips@fbi.gov, by contacting your local field office, if in the United States, or by contacting the nearest U.S. Embassy, if located overseas. More information about the Tymoshchuk TOC reward offer and one related to Hive ransomware is located on the State Department website.

In a recent development, CCIPS investigates and prosecutes cybercrime and intellectual property (IP) crime in coordination with domestic and international law enforcement agencies, often with assistance from the private sector. Since 2020, CCIPS has secured the conviction of over 180 cyber and IP criminals, and court orders for the return of over $350 million in victim funds.

Nobody enjoys thinking about serious illness in a pet, and itâs natural to want to look the other way. But considering many serious feline health conditions respond well to early intervention, a little knowledge can go a long way. Here are eight of the most serious, what they tend to look like, and practical steps that can help lower the risk. The aim isnât to worry anyone, just to help owners feel prepared.

Heart problems are notoriously hard to spot in cats, even during a routine health check, because the usual signs, like a murmur, donât always show up during an exam. The most common form of cardiac disease â hypertrophic cardiomyopathy â causes the heart muscle to thicken so it canât work as well, and it can cause sudden death. Vets rely on heart scans, chest X-rays, and blood tests to discover heart disease.

Lowering the risk: Genetics play a massive part, so anyone buying a kitten from a breeder should ask whether the parentsâ hearts have been checked, particularly if your breed of choice is one with a higher incidence of cardiac disease, like purebred Maine Coons, Siamese, Sphynx, Ragdoll, and Burmese. A high-quality, nutritionally balanced diet formulated for cats is a vital ingredient in promoting heart health. Cat food must contain the amino acid taurine because cats cannot make it themselves, and a diet lacking this essential nutrient is a fast track to heart disease.

Kidney disease is common in older cats. The kidneys slowly lose their ability to filter waste, which highlights up as drinking and urinating more, tiredness, weight loss, and a scruffy coat. It can also lead to high blood pressure and low red blood cell counts, which cause pale gums, weakness, and fast breathing.

Lowering the risk: Although kidney disease canât be entirely prevented, regular checkups with blood and urine tests can catch changes early. A balanced diet helps, and maximizing a catâs water intake by feeding wet food and providing a range of enticing water options can make a significant difference.

Recent findings suggest that feline Leukemia Virus (FeLV) is prevalent in cat populations around the world and is the most common cause of feline cancer. FeLV attacks the bone marrow, and the clinical signs of infection can be quite variable, but often include lethargy, weight loss, poor appetite, and weakness. Because FeLV cripples the immune system, affected cats are more susceptible to disease, and an otherwise simple infection can be deadly.

According to recent reports, lowering the risk: Vaccination is the best protection. Keeping cats indoors and away from possibly infected cats helps, as does quarantining newcomers and regularly cleaning dishes, toys, bedding, and litter boxes.

Recent findings suggest that this is the most common hormone disease in cats, affecting about 10% of cats over age ten. It can lead to heart problems, kidney disease, blindness, and death. Cats lose weight promptly despite a huge appetite, and some suddenly go blind because of high blood pressure. Fortunately, the outlook is good with treatment, including medication, surgery, or radioactive iodine.

Lowering the risk: Hyperthyroidism canât be prevented, so spotting changes early and getting annual blood screening are the best weapons.

Up to one in a hundred cats develops diabetes in their lifetime, either because they donât make enough insulin or canât use it properly. Left untreated, it can cause serious complications. Signs include weight loss, drinking and urinating more, accidents outside the litter box, and bloody urine. Treatment is usually insulin injections, but if caught early, it can sometimes be managed through diet.

It has been revealed that lowering the risk: Feeding a high-quality, nutritionally balanced diet with low carbohydrate levels can help reduce the risks. The most common form of diabetes in cats is Type 2 (insulin resistance) and the best way to avoid this disease is by maintaining a lean, healthy body condition.

Sources indicate that rabies is almost always fatal, and cats are the domestic animal most likely to get it. It spreads through bites and scratches, often from wildlife such as bats, skunks, raccoons, and foxes. Some infected cats become withdrawn, others irritable or aggressive, and drooling and wide pupils are common. It is dangerous for people too.

Lowering the risk: Vaccines protect for one to three years. If contact with rabies is suspected, veterinary attention must be sought immediately. The disease is invariably fatal once clinical signs of rabies appear, so donât wait.

In a recent development, feline Infectious Peritonitis (FIP) is caused by a mutated form of feline coronavirus. Early signs are mild, such as tiredness, but many cats develop a swollen belly from fluid, and it can progress fast. Until recently, FIP was almost always fatal, though newer treatments are changing this.

In a recent development, lowering the risk: Good hygiene between cats and isolating newcomers until theyâre healthy reduce exposure. Keeping cats healthy and up to date on other vaccines may also help.

According to recent reports, spread by mosquitoes, heartworms are less common in cats than in dogs, but they can still cause serious disease, including sudden death. Wheezing and coughing are the most common signs, and the infection is hard to detect.

Lowering the risk: A monthly preventive is the best defense. If you live in an area where heartworm is present, it takes only one mosquito, so even indoor cats can be exposed.

Recent findings suggest that not every disease on this list can be prevented, but many can be avoided or managed simply by providing your cat with a high-quality diet and keeping up with regular vet checks. Blood and urine tests, appropriate vaccines, and monthly flea, tick, and heartworm protection all help, and keeping cats indoors lowers exposure to injury and illness. Catching problems early is often what makes treatment most effective, and a vet can help tailor a initiative for each cat.

According to recent reports, the Sato Project rescues dogs in Puerto Rico and helps place them in homes, including in the northeastern United States. Some arrive with limited information about their histories, and assumptions about a dogâs background can influence how potential adopters perceive them.

A dogâs history can help rescue teams understand what support an animal may need and how to approach introductions to a new home. But the past doesnât tell the whole story. A complicated backstory might tell us where a dog has been. It doesnât tell us everything about who they are. Dogs, much like people, are so much more than their basic profile.

Industry observers note that dogs respond to the world as individuals. One may eagerly approach a stranger, while another prefers to observe from a safe distance. It has been revealed that the Rescue Collection offers a different starting point. That first spark of interest can matter, especially for dogs who might otherwise be overlooked.

Dogs explore their surroundings through several senses, and their behavior around unfamiliar objects can offer clues about what attracts their attention. But interpreting those responses requires care.

It has been revealed that dogs also see color differently from humans. People typically have three types of color-sensitive cone cells in their retinas, while dogs have two, a form of vision known as dichromacy. Dogs distinguish blues and yellows relatively well but have more difficulty differentiating reds and greens. Their visual experience of the world is therefore different from ours.

That doesnât mean dogs see the world in black and white. Color is only one possible influence on how they respond to an object. Shape, contrast, texture, scent, movement, and the surrounding environment may also play a part.

Nor does spending longer near a sculpture necessarily mean a dog prefers its artistic style. The dog may be interested in its shape or position, or simply feel comfortable resting there.

In a recent development, A single gallery visit cannot establish an animalâs overall personality or predict how they will behave around children, other dogs, or visitors at home. Behavior is best understood across time and situations.

Recent findings suggest that A sculpture might have us admiring its color and form. The dog? They might be more interested in giving it a sniff. Different critics, different criteria.

In a recent development, although the profiles are not scientific personality assessments or guarantees of compatibility, they do invite us to learn more about each dog. Conversations with the rescue team and time spent meeting the dog remain essential to finding a suitable match.

Rescue work involves far more than finding adopters. Veterinary care, foster placements, transportation, behavioral support, and follow-up all require time and resources. Helping the public connect with the dogs is only one part of that work, but an vital one.

It has been revealed that the Sato Projectâs adoption and foster manager, Alessandra Migliore, said the organization was excited to explore new ways of showcasing its dogsâ personalities. Industry News: You Don't Need a Greenhouse – These 6 Clever Tricks Help Protect Winter Vegetables From Frost

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that your greens look great on Sunday afternoon.
  • Industry observers note that several of the cold-hardy winter vegetables keep producing through the colder months, and a greenhouse isn't required to help them along.
  • Industry observers note that A handful of frosty nights in November is a different problem from weeks of frozen ground.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that your greens look great on Sunday afternoon. Then a clear, still night pulls the temperature down hard, and by Monday morning the lettuce has gone dark and limp, and the chard leaves look soft and water-soaked. It's a rough way to lose a bed of winter vegetables you've been tending since late summer, especially when the forecast only mentioned a light frost.

Industry observers note that several of the cold-hardy winter vegetables keep producing through the colder months, and a greenhouse isn't required to help them along. Cheap covers and a little attention on cold evenings go a long way, and a good share of the materials are probably in the garage already.

Industry observers note that A handful of frosty nights in November is a different problem from weeks of frozen ground. Light covers can usually handle the first. That second one takes layers – fabric over the plants, mulch over the soil, and sometimes a solid structure on top.

Row covers get sold as frost blankets or horticultural fleece, but it's the same thin spun fabric either way. Light, air, and rain get through. What it holds in is warmth rising from the soil overnight, usually enough to keep lettuce, spinach, kale, and Swiss chard a few degrees warmer than bare beds. Heavy 1.5-ounce (51g/m²) cover holds more heat. It also blocks about half the light, so keep it for cold snaps.

In a recent development, heat leaks out at the edges, so the cover has to touch the ground all the way around. Boards, bricks, or smooth rocks hold it down. If it sags onto tender leaves, slide a few hoops under it (see section 3). A row or two fits under the Agfabric 1.2-ounce frost cloth from Home Depot, a 10-by-50-foot (3 by 15 m) roll.

In a recent development, cut the bottom out of an empty gallon (3.8L) milk jug, and it'll turn into a mini DIY greenhouse for a young lettuce or spinach plant. Smaller seedlings will get by under a soda bottle. Shove the cut edge into the dirt and pile soil around it, or it'll likely end up in the neighbor's yard after the first windy night. Then check that no leaves press on the plastic.

Your jug's cap comes off, too. Sealed up, a jug warms fast on a sunny afternoon, and the seedling can overheat while you're still outside in a jacket. Lift the jugs off on mild, bright days and drop them back on at dusk. If you run short on jugs, reusable clear plastic bell cloches, like these Senwell cloches from Amazon, go on the same way. They come with metal ground stakes to keep them in place.

It has been revealed that bend flexible ½-inch (1.3 cm) PVC pipe or heavy wire into hoops about 4 feet (1.2 m) apart over a bed, then stretch frost fabric or clear greenhouse plastic across the top. One tunnel can shelter a whole raised bed or a long row of greens. A Haxnicks fleece tunnel from Walmart comes with the steel hoops already attached and stretches to about 10 feet (3 m).

So should it get fabric or plastic? Fabric is the low-fuss choice, since air moves through it and it can stay on for days. Plastic gets warmer in the daytime and sheds rain, but after dark it's no warmer than fabric. Closed plastic can cook the greens on a bright afternoon, so pull up a side or open the ends. Wet, heavy snow can flatten it, too. Snowy areas need sturdier hoops set closer together, plus a brush-off after each storm.

You can leave carrots, parsnips, and other root crops in the bed past fall. Heap straw or shredded leaves on the row, and many of them will keep until you want them. Soil under that pile doesn't freeze as deep or flip between frozen and thawed as often. Left in over winter, a parsnip is, honestly, a sweeter parsnip come spring. Dig the rest before they bolt.

Mulch only protects the soil, though – it won't keep exposed kale or chard leaves from freezing on a hard night, so pair it with a cover. Be picky about the straw, too. Hay and bargain bales can be full of weed seed. GardenStraw wheat straw mulch from Lowe's is filtered, with most of the seed screened out, in a 2-cubic-foot (57L) box.

Sources indicate that an old storm window in the garage is halfway to a cold frame. Hinge it to the back of a bottomless wooden box, or right onto a raised bed. Inside, it can run 10 to 20°F (6 to 11°C) warmer than the open garden. Spinach, mâche, and winter lettuce do well in one. Backyard Discovery's cedar cold frame from Walmart has a lid that lifts on its own once the inside passes 70°F (21°C).

Glass is heavy and can break, so secure the pane firmly so a gust can't slam it, and sand any sharp edges. Windows painted before 1978 may also contain lead paint – not something you want flaking into a food bed. On sunny days, heat is the bigger risk, so prop the lid open. Tuck a sensor like this AcuRite wireless thermometer from Lowe's inside the frame, and check it from the house.

According to recent reports, pots give you an option a bed doesn't. Their weak spot is down in the roots. Those are usually far less cold-hardy than the leaves, and a pot doesn't give them much soil for cover, so a freeze reaches them faster than roots in the ground. Still, you can pick up a pot of parsley, kale, or salad greens and carry it somewhere better. Crowd them by a wall the wind doesn't hit and throw burlap or bubble wrap around the bunch.

Sources indicate that water them well the day before a hard freeze. Wet soil freezes more slowly than dry soil, it turns out. On the bitter nights, carry the smaller ones into an unheated garage or shed. Get them back out the next morning, or once that cold spell is over. Greens left in a dim garage for days can come out pale and leggy.

Kale, collards, spinach, parsley, and cabbage can take a lot. Frost under 28°F (-2°C) usually doesn't bother them, but when the forecast calls for low 20°s F (around -6°C), cover them anyway. Lettuce, Swiss chard, beets, and carrots aren't quite as tough. Damage can show up in the mid- to upper 20°s (about -4 to -2°C). Mâche is the odd one out among salad greens and holds up better than lettuce. Beans, peppers, and tomatoes can't take even a light frost.

Industry observers note that these ratings aren't fixed, though. Two varieties of the same crop can differ in hardiness, and an established kale plant usually gets through a freeze in better shape than one transplanted last week. Plants that have had several weeks of slowly cooling weather also hold up better than ones hit by a hard freeze after a warm spell. Watch how long the cold lasts, not just how low it'll go.

A greenhouse would be nice, sure, but straw over the carrots, fabric over the kale, and a couple of milk jugs over the late lettuce will carry a garden a long way. Keep a frost blanket folded by the back door. The night the forecast suddenly drops, it'll be the first thing you reach for.

It has been revealed that tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

Snickers is a calico cat born in Owensboro, Kentucky, USA, whose adorable âsmileâ has hundreds of thousands of fans. Her life journey hasnât always been smooth, but this remarkable cat touches the heart of every person she meets along the way. It was her fierce personality that inspired her pawrent, Kelly DeWeese, to go to great lengths to ensure Snickers gets to live her best life.

June 2020 was a challenging time for Kelly. She had recently lost her mother, leaving her in a state of grief, and in an attempt to find solace and cope with her loss, she took up running. It was during one of these runs, only her second, that a tiny, fragile kitten crossed her path.

According to recent reports, kelly was jogging past vast cornfields, and her mind was hyper-focused on the pleasing sound of the stalks rustling in the wind when a small calico kitten appeared out of the blue. She was alone, sick, and desperately in need of help.

Snickers, as she would later be christened, was in terrible shape. Her eyes were crusted shut; she couldn't meow, and she had severe respiratory problems, including sneezing. Her frail body was covered in fleas, and it was clear she was suffering.

In a recent development, moved by compassion, Kelly scooped up the little kitten and carried her the two miles back to her home, where she was given a much-needed bath and plenty of TLC. The following day, Kelly took her to the local veterinarian, who ran various tests and initiated a series of treatments.

Despite the efforts of the local vet, the situation didn't improve, and the bills were mounting. Snickers' condition was dire.

Despite the financial strain, Kelly's determination to save Snickers was unwavering. After several trips to the vet, it became clear that this brave little kitten needed specialized care. Snickers was referred to a specialist in Louisville, Kentucky, two hours away. There, a CT scan revealed the root of her health issues: large polyps behind her eyes and deep within her inner ear.

The specialist recommended two major surgeries to remove the polyps. The surgeries were spaced six weeks apart and were extremely expensive. The first surgery was a great success, but the second operation had a life-altering consequence. During the procedure, one of the polyps slipped into her neck, temporarily cutting off oxygen to the brain. She essentially died for a few seconds before the surgical team managed to resuscitate her with CPR. Tragically, Snickers woke up from the operation blind.

The prognosis was uncertain, with a 50/50 chance of her regaining her eyesight. But Kelly, determined and resolute, refused to give up on her beloved feline companion. She watched over Snickers as she adjusted to her newfound blindness, never losing hope.

Remarkably, a couple of months later, a miracle occurred. One day, while she was waving something in front of Snickers, the catâs reaction gave Kelly a glimmer of hope. It appeared that Snickers might be regaining her eyesight. Ecstatic about this newfound possibility, Kelly promptly took Snickers back to the specialist, who confirmed the miraculous news: Snickers had indeed regained her eyesight.

Recent findings suggest that now, Snickers is a thriving and healthy six-year-old cat, bearing her distinctive, always-smiling face. Her remarkable journey from a sickly, abandoned kitten to a joyful, beloved family member is a testament to the power of love and determination. Her infectious smile serves as a constant reminder that sometimes, in the face of adversity, the most extraordinary things can happen. Kelly's unyielding commitment to Snickers proves that every life, no matter how small, is worth fighting for.

Sources indicate that all those present at the veterinary clinic will agree that Snickers' recovery was nothing short of a miracle, and her journey to health and happiness continued to inspire those who heard her story. Sources indicate that dogster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn a commission at no cost to you. Read about privacy.

For years, business owners and property managers have wrestled with the same question: how do you tell the difference between a legitimate service animal and a pet that someone is trying to pass off as one?

Itâs a question John Bradford spent years trying to answer, first as a property manager overseeing thousands of rental units, and now as the founder of PetScreening, a platform used to verify animal accommodation requests across more than 7 million rental units nationwide.

With the rising number of service dogs and emotional support animals leading to incidents of confusion, conflict, and exploitation, John sets the record straight on how to verify a real service animal from one that isn't, and what you are legally allowed to ask.

Sources indicate that the truth is that most people donât fully understand the laws around service animals and emotional support animals, and even well-meaning questions can come across as anything but. That gray area and confusion can create real risk. Ask the wrong question, and a business can face a discrimination complaint. Ask no questions at all, and policies and rules become easy to bend, which leads to potentially dangerous situations.

Getting this right protects everyone involved, including the people who genuinely rely on these animals every day.

Under the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), service animals are defined as:.

âDogs that are individually trained to do work or perform tasks for people with disabilities.â.

It has been revealed that disabilities vary widely, from physical and sensory to psychiatric, intellectual, and neurological. The needs of each person are different, so the trained tasks may look different from person to person. The ADA cites that the service animal must be a dog or, in rare cases, a miniature horse. Federal law does not require certifications, registrations, vests, or ID cards for these animals.

In a recent development, beyond the specification that the animal must be trained to perform tasks, the legal standard is limited, so it can be difficult to easily identify which animals are legitimately service dogs and which are not. This is where public confusion starts.

According to recent reports, there are plenty of ways to make a dog look like a service animal, like labeled vests, âregistrationâ certifications, and IDs, but none of these are federally supported. A dog wearing a vest isnât automatically a service animal, and a dog without one isnât automatically a pet. What matters legally is not appearance or paperwork. Itâs the dogâs trained ability to perform certain tasks.

Industry observers note that this is the distinction many find hardest to grasp, and it matters because different laws apply to each. Service dogs are protected under the ADA and, due to their training and the tasks they perform, they are permitted in public spaces such as restaurants, retail stores, and hotels. That could mean guiding someone who is visually impaired, alerting an owner to an oncoming seizure, or reminding them to take medication. Service animals are also protected under the Fair Housing Act and require paperwork if the disability or need for the animal is not obviously understood.

Recent findings suggest that emotional support animals (ESAs) are different. Their value comes from the comfort their presence provides. They donât necessarily have to be dogs, they arenât required to be trained to perform specific tasks, and theyâre not covered by the ADA to be allowed in public spaces like restaurants.

Recent findings suggest that they are, however, protected by the Fair Housing Act. Under this, landlords are generally required to make allowances for an ESA if a tenant has appropriate documentation from a licensed healthcare provider establishing a disability-related need. Examples of disabilities warranting an ESA include, but are not limited to, anxiety disorders or autism.

In a recent development, ESA accommodations are supposed to come through legitimate means, typically an established relationship with a licensed medical or mental health professional who can document the need. But some people have found loopholes for this by filling out forms online or paying fees for instant letters, which only fuels public skepticism about the legitimate need for these animals. Not to mention, this abuse can make people wary of service dogs, too.

While there is no foolproof visual test, trained service animals typically display consistent, recognizable behaviors. These dogs show exemplary discipline and obedience to the commands of their handler. They have the ability to ignore external distractions from other dogs, people, food, sounds, and smells while focusing on the needs of their handler. They display a calm temperament and are not aggressive or anxious. It is also expected that these animals be quiet, unless they are tasked with alerting an owner to a medical issue, and that they are housebroken and trained to walk on a leash without unnecessary pulling or circling.

Sources indicate that this is where business owners and landlords need to tread carefully. When it isnât obvious that a dog is a service animal, staff are permitted to ask:.

Is this dog required because of a disability?

What task has it been trained to perform?

In a recent development, thatâs the full extent of it. Staff should not ask about the nature of a personâs disability, demand documentation or proof of training, or require dogs to demonstrate their tasks. Asking beyond the two questions, even if it comes from a place of genuine curiosity or caution, can expose a business to discrimination claims.

In a recent development, news stories about supposed service animals harming bystanders in public continue to raise questions about the legitimacy of those animals, and businesses are often caught in the crossfire. These incidents are symptoms of a larger problem: businesses and property owners navigating without clear guidance, while people with legitimate needs are met with suspicion.

Service animals and emotional support animals play an essential role in the lives of the people who rely on them, and protecting that role starts with understanding the rules.

If you own a business or manage a property, you donât need to become legal experts overnight, but you do need a consistent, fair process that respects peopleâs rights and keeps everyone safe. When everyone knows where the lines are, the people who truly depend on these animals can go about their lives without facing doubt at every door.

The 6 Beautiful but Messy Trees That Will Leave You With Hours of Cleanup – and What to Plant Instead

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that but it’s key to slow down a bit and figure out if that tree is...
  • It has been revealed that honestly, the messiest trees might promise the world, but they are sure to make your life infinitely more difficult, perhaps dropping spiky seed balls or spreading thousands of unwanted seedlings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most of us do not have unlimited free time to garden. That’s why terms like “easy-care” and “drought-tolerant” can make a shrub so appealing. And if the tree characterized as “easy-care” is also gorgeous, it has a good chance of finding its way into our garden.

It has been revealed that but it’s key to slow down a bit and figure out if that tree is... well, if it's messy. Messy trees can be easy enough to grow, but you may be signing yourself up for relentless cleanup – and some stunning ornamentals that light up your landscape may create far more work for you than you realize.

It has been revealed that honestly, the messiest trees might promise the world, but they are sure to make your life infinitely more difficult, perhaps dropping spiky seed balls or spreading thousands of unwanted seedlings. And garden stores know better than to stick a “messy” label on them.

It has been revealed that keen to swerve the cleanup? Well, Gardening Know How is here to help!

Sources indicate that we’ve identified six of the messiest trees around (none of which happen to be your birth month tree, thankfully) and we’re here to rat them out. We’ll outline the features of each that will win your heart, as well as what they do to earn their “messy” status, plus an equally beautiful, less messy alternative. You're welcome.

Ah the ginkgo. It’s hard to add this fabulous, ancient tree to the “messy” list given its incredible history; after all, its lineage dates back over 270 million years, and it is known as a “living fossil” because, for years, botanists believed that the tree was extinct. They found fossil evidence of its unique, fan-shaped leaves, but nary a living tree was found for years. Then, one day in the 1600s, a small grove was located in a temple garden in Japan and the world got ginkgos again.

Recent findings suggest that these are wonderful, noble trees with leaves that blaze gold in the autumn. However, do not invite one into your landscape until you are assured that it is a male. Female ginkgos make the “messy” list because they drop oodles of fleshy, cherry-sized fruit that smell like rotting flesh when crushed. You’ll be cleaning up and holding your nose for a month.

Recent findings suggest that plant instead: a male gingko. There are cultivars that are all-male (like this beautiful Autumn Gold Ginkgo Tree from Nature Hills) and this is not the time to demand gender equality!

Industry observers note that eastern cottonwood is a messy tree with a lot to recommend it. It is a fast-growing, deciduous tree, large and impressive, sometimes reaching 150 ft tall. It plays a critical role in the ecosystem, supporting 249 caterpillar species (including your birth month caterpillar). It is also lovely, with flat leaf stems that catch even the lightest breeze, causing the heart-shaped leaves to shimmer and rustle.

According to recent reports, but look out below! Every year a female cottonwood produces a massive volume of tiny seeds wrapped in sticky white, cotton-like fibers that blanket lawns, clog gutters, and wrap around air conditioners.

Sources indicate that plant instead: the Chinese pistache. If you long for a large shade tree but want to avoid cottonwood's fluffy seeds, plant a Chinese pistache like this one from Brighter Blooms. It grows more slowly and fits in well in residential gardens.

According to recent reports, southern magnolias are the belles of the ball in the landscape, with their goblet-shaped, intensely fragrant white blooms and large, glossy leaves. The trees are evergreens that can grow above 60 feet (20m) tall and half that wide. They have a real presence in the garden.

It has been revealed that but don’t fall for this pretty face until you learn of the work you will be required to do to keep your garden looking good. Southern magnolia trees shed, and they shed almost constantly. They shed their heavy waxy leaves; they shed their large seed cones; and they shed spent petals. Picking up in a year-round job.

Recent findings suggest that plant instead: flowering dogwood. If you love the Southern magnolia’s showy flowers, sub in a flowering dogwood (aka the tree quietly replacing magnolias everywhere). It is a more manageable size with lovely white “flowers” that are actually bracts.

A post shared by Vikram Baliga (@the.plant.prof).

The gorgeous cloud of white spring flowers has turned many a head, and the Bradford pear (despite the controversy surrounding it) is widely used as a street tree and even in gardens. It offers a graceful, symmetrical shape, pretty spring blossoms, and lively fall foliage.

Industry observers note that however, best enjoy looking at this little flowering tree in someone else’s yard, because those white flowers that look like they were cultivated by angels actually smell awful! Some liken the odor to rotting fish, others to sweaty foot fungus. This happens when the tree is in full bloom, and the petals hold onto the smell as they fall.

Recent findings suggest that plant instead: a wild cherry (Prunus avium). Like the Bradford pear, a cherry erupts in clusters of stunning white flowers just as spring rolls in. But something like the Montmorency Cherry Tree from Nature Hills is a native and its blossoms smell like flowers instead of fish. Those flowers produce fruit that is loved by local birds.

Oh the autumn color you’ll enjoy with a sweetgum tree! This fast-growing native tree has lovely starry leaves that turn all sorts of fiery colors before they fall. Each leaf has five to seven lobes that turn orange, crimson, and purple in autumn. A sweetgum is a tolerant tree, accepting heat, drought, and soil compaction, as well as feeding birds in winter.

But sweetgum has its downsides: primarily, the hard, spiky "gumballs" that hurt bare feet and make mowing difficult. Yes, this lovely tree drops thousands of woody seed pods from winter through spring. They hurt your feet if you walk barefoot, and even with shoes on, they can trip you up and cause ankle injuries. They even destroy lawnmower blades. Yet they are really difficult to rake up.

Plant instead: red maple (Acer rubrum). If you want a tree for fall color and shade, a seedless red maple cultivar will treat you right. It offers similar shade and a brilliant red or orange autumn display and similar shade.

It has been revealed that what a mix! Crabapples offer spectacular spring flowers and attractive berries. They are small trees, usually under 25 feet (8m) tall, grown for their ornamental beauty and wildlife value.

However, if you get a messy crabapple variety, you may come to regret inviting the tree into your landscape. The large, juicy fruits fall readily from the tree and make the ground below a slippery mess. Having to trudge through the slippery rotting fruits is icky and even dangerous, but cleaning up cannot be called fun wither.

Sources indicate that plant instead: a “clean” variety of crabapple. You can select a fruitless variety like Spring Snow Crabapple (Malus 'Spring Snow'), with dense clusters of fragrant, pure white blossoms in mid-spring. Or, if you prefer, a Prairifire Flowering Crabapple Tree from Nature Hills, which promises to be far too tempting to local birds to ever spill a berry.

Sources indicate that of course, if you have the time to do the cleanup, then there's no harm planting a messy tree in your yard. Just be sure you're willing to roll your sleeves up and get cracking when things get mucky – and if not, one of our beautiful alternatives is definitely the better choice for you.

According to recent reports, teo Spengler is a master gardener and a docent at the San Francisco Botanical Garden, where she hosts public tours. She has studied horticulture and written about nature, trees, plants and gardening for more than two decades. Before turning her focus to gardening, she worked as an attorney and legal writer, experience she also brings to her role as our Gardening Lawyer. Her extended family includes some 30 houseplants and hundreds of outdoor plants, including 250 trees, which are her main passion. Spengler at the moment splits her life between San Francisco and the French Basque Country, though she was raised in Alaska, giving her experience of gardening in a range of climates.

According to recent reports, my dog, Reggie, has Cherry eye. If left untreated, can it have a negative effect on his vision? Money is an issue for me right now.â.

Cherry eye happens when the gland of the third eyelid, which helps produce tears, slips out of its normal position and becomes visible as a pink or red cherry-looking bulge in the corner of your dog's eye. I understand that veterinary expenses can be difficult to manage, and it is important to know what needs attention right away and what can safely wait a bit longer.

Cherry eye does not usually cause blindness directly, but leaving it untreated can put Reggie's eye health at risk. The exposed gland can become irritated, inflamed, or damaged, and its tear production may be reduced over time. Because this gland contributes to keeping the eye moist and protected, reduced tear production can increase the risk of dry eye, a condition that can lead to corneal damage, scarring, and impaired vision if it becomes severe. Think of the gland as part of the eye's built-in lubrication system. Even if the eye looks comfortable today, problems can develop gradually.

If surgery is not financially possible right now, please arrange a veterinary examination to confirm the diagnosis, assess tear production, and check the cornea.

Recent findings suggest that talk to your vet about a payment blueprint, or you might be able to find a veterinary teaching hospital or nonprofit clinic that may offer lower-cost care. Your veterinarian may recommend a suitable lubricating eye product while you work toward surgery, but lubrication will not reposition the gland. Please make sure you avoid human eye drops, leftover medications, or steroid eye drops unless specifically prescribed, as some of these can worsen an undiagnosed corneal ulcer. The gland should generally be repositioned and preserved rather than removed. If the gland is removed, you would need to use eye drops to supplement Reggieâs tear production for the rest of his life.

Please seek same-day veterinary care if you see Reggie squinting, holding the eye closed, rubbing it persistently, developing a cloudy or bluish cornea, or producing thick yellow or green discharge. These can be signs of a painful or more serious eye problem. If the eye is comfortable and clear, it may not be an immediate emergency, but I would not leave cherry eye unassessed for weeks or months. The most important first step is protecting the eye while finding an affordable treatment option.

I know, I know; poinsettias are absolutely the traditional choice for festive decorating, but there's another festive container plant that deserves a place by your front door this winter.

One of those underrated beauties that deserves its time in the spotlight, this holiday plant may not have the bold and colorful bracts of a classic poinsettia, but what it lacks in showy flowers, it more than makes up for in fragrance, evergreen foliage and year-round appeal.

In fact, if you're looking for a festive container plant that keeps on giving long after the holiday decorations have come down, it could be just the thing you're looking for (and then some!).

It has been revealed that poinsettias are practically synonymous with the holidays, and little wonder; their bright red, pink or white foliage brings an instant splash of festive color. Still, there's no getting away from the fact that their appeal is largely seasonal. They're tender plants, usually grown indoors in the US, and need warmth, bright indirect light, careful watering, and lots of TLC to keep them looking their best.

Once the holidays are over and those colorful bracts begin to fade, many poinsettias end up in the compost or trash. And, while it's possible to keep them growing and even encourage them to develop their colorful bracts again the following year, doing so takes a little effort.

Enter stage left, then, the beautiful sweet box (Sarcococca).

Sources indicate that obviously, sweet box offers a rather different proposition, as this handsome evergreen shrub doesn't have to be replaced when Christmas is over. In fact, its glossy leaves provide structure and greenery throughout the year, while its winter flowers bring a welcome surprise just when the garden can feel at its dullest.

And it's not just about looks, either! Sweet box has a secret weapon that poinsettias simply can't compete with: its extraordinary perfume.

That's right, folks; sweet box produces masses of creamy-white flowers in winter, often tucked discreetly beneath its glossy leaves. They might not look particularly impressive from a distance, but get close and you'll discover why this shrub is so treasured, as they release a perfume often described as a combination of vanilla and jasmine.

It's surprisingly powerful for such delicate blooms, and on a still winter day, the scent can drift through the garden and greet you as you approach your front door. Especially if you opt for a variety like the Sweet & Lo™ Sweet Box from Proven Winners.

Recent findings suggest that once flowering finishes, sweet box can produce ornamental berries, which mature from red to dark purple or black depending on the species and variety. And it does all of this while standing in partial or full shade, no less!

Although some sweet box varieties can eventually become quite substantial shrubs, its slow-growing nature also makes it a useful long-term container plant. (You won't be constantly battling to keep it in shape, for starters, although a light trim after flowering can help maintain a neat outline if needed).

Just be sure to choose a pot with drainage holes and use a good moisture-retentive potting mix. Pop it somewhere sheltered in partial or full shade, and water when the compost begins to dry – just like all container-grown plants, it will need a little more attention to watering than those growing in the ground, particularly during dry spells.

Of course, there's nothing wrong with a beautiful poinsettia, but if you'd rather invest in a plant that offers more than a few weeks of seasonal color, sweet box is well worth your time... not to mention a place in your heart. Not least of all because it's the sort of hard-working hero plant that continues to provide beauty long after the festive season has passed.

If your home and garden is full of those awkward shady spots where other plants might struggle, then, look no further! And if not? Well, still show it some love, I say – for a festive container with fragrance, character and staying power, sweet box is a very hard plant to beat.

In a recent development, genetics can contribute, too. Inherited tendencies may influence a dog's motivation to chase, retrieve, explore, or seek food. But a predisposition doesn't guarantee a particular behavior, nor does it explain every individual habit. A dog's behavior comes from a combination of biology and learned experience, which is often less convenient than blaming everything on their breed, but it is much closer to reality.

A 2022 study published in Science looked at the behavior and DNA of thousands of dogs. Researchers found that a dog's breed explained only about 9% of the differences in behavior between individual dogs. In other words, dogs of the same breed can have very different personalities and behaviors. Genetics plays a role, but it doesn't tell the whole story.

That doesn't mean genetics is irrelevant. The researchers found evidence that many behavioral traits do have a heritable component. Rather, the findings show why breed alone is a poor crystal ball for predicting how an individual dog will behave.

The bed itself can be exciting, particularly because it smells like a favorite person and offers a chance for interaction. In other cases, a dog may simply have energy left to burn. Understanding the possible reasons can help explain why bedtime sometimes turns into playtime.

Sources indicate that dogs spend much of their time looking up at people from the floor. Climbing onto a bed changes that perspective, bringing a dog much closer to its owner's face and making interaction easier.

That alone can be enough to spark a playful mood. A dog may drop into a play bow, bark for attention, or bounce around in an attempt to encourage its person to join in.

Being face to face can make play feel more inviting, particularly for dogs that enjoy close interaction with their owners. What looks like a sudden burst of energy may simply be a dog making the most of the opportunity to engage on a different level.

Sources indicate that A bed carries the scent of the person who sleeps in it, making it an especially interesting place for a dog to explore. Dogs rely heavily on their noses to understand their surroundings, and familiar smells can be particularly appealing.

For a dog that enjoys spending time with its owner, the bed may be one of the most comforting and interesting places in the home. Rolling around on the sheets or sniffing the blankets lets a dog investigate those familiar scents while enjoying a spot associated with its favorite person.

That combination of comfort, familiarity, and excitement can help explain why some dogs become especially playful once they climb onto the mattress.

It has been revealed that for dogs that love burrowing, a bed covered in sheets and blankets can feel like an invitation to play. Digging, wriggling underneath the covers, and pushing through folds of fabric can all become part of the fun.

Some breeds are particularly inclined toward this kind of behavior. Dachshunds, for example, were bred to pursue animals such as badgers and weasels into their burrows. Their instinct to dig and tunnel can make a pile of blankets especially appealing. Meanwhile, Chihuahuas seem to be particularly fond of burrowing into the warmth and security of their humanâs bed.

A dog that discovers the pleasure of diving between the sheets may quickly turn it into a regular bedtime activity.

According to recent reports, bedtime can also signal that the day is winding down and an opportunity for cuddling is approaching. A dog that enjoys being close to its owner may become excited at the prospect of spending that time together.

If playful behavior consistently earns attention, a dog may be encouraged to repeat it. What begins as a burst of excitement can become a familiar part of the nightly routine. Even if this nightly ritual isnât one you welcome, waving arms and raised voices often count as a positive interaction for a dog, so if youâre trying to get your dog off the bed, be careful your methods align with your message.

Sometimes, a dog becomes especially energetic at bedtime simply because theyâre not ready to settle down. If it hasn't had enough exercise or stimulation during the day, the bed may become an outlet for that leftover energy.

A dog that is still eager to run, jump, and play may need more activity before the household turns in for the night. An evening walk or a game of tug-of-war can help provide an opportunity to burn off some energy before bedtime.

A dog that's had enough exercise and stimulation is more likely to be ready to relax, rather than treating the mattress as a playground.

According to recent reports, many owners enjoy sleeping alongside their dogs, while others prefer to keep their beds pet-free. Sharing a bed can feel cozy and comforting, and having a dog nearby may also be soothing for people who experience anxiety or other mental health challenges.

There are practical considerations, too. Dogs can carry dirt, bacteria, and parasites into the bed, and some owners would rather not have fur on their sheets or pillows.

Recent findings suggest that ultimately, whether a dog is allowed to sleep on the bed comes down to what works for the household. If itâs not a problem, then itâs not a problem. There's no single right choice, and a dog can still enjoy plenty of affection and companionship without sharing the mattress.

If you do want your bed to be a dog-free zone, the simplest solution is to keep the bedroom door closed. But if youâre simply looking for a way to get them off the bed without it turning into a party, a calm and quiet approach is best. A single command or using a slip-lead to silently guide them off the bed will be far more effective than shouting and pointing.

Sources indicate that A dog getting frisky on the bed is often responding to a combination of familiar scents, opportunities for attention, and the chance to play somewhere comfortable. Blankets can add to the appeal, especially for dogs that enjoy burrowing.

According to recent reports, if the behavior seems excessive, however, it may be worth looking at how much exercise and stimulation the dog gets during the day. Adding a walk or play session before bed can help make the transition to sleep easier.

According to recent reports, for many dogs, the bed is simply an exciting place to be close to their favorite person. With a little preparation, bedtime can still end in a peaceful night's sleep rather than an impromptu wrestling match.

#9226. What Your Orchid Needs in November for Spectacular Winter Blooms – 6 Easy Tasks to Do Now
